meaning_mnemonic: Lying on the ground is something that looks just like the ground, the number One. Why is this One lying down? It's been shot by the number two. It's lying there, bleeding out and dying. The number One doesn't have long to live.
reading_mnemonic: As you're sitting there next to One, holding him up, you start feeling a weird sensation all over your skin. From the wound comes a fine powder (obviously coming from the special bullet used to kill One) that causes the person it touches to get extremely itchy (いち).

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji two and the radical two are the exact same things. Therefore, you know the kanji for two already!
reading_mnemonic: How do you count to two? Just use someone's knee (に), and then their other knee. There — two knees!

meaning_mnemonic: Nice! This kanji is the same as the radical that looks just like it (down to the meaning, even!). The radical is nine and the kanji is nine, making the meaning of this kanji really easy to remember as long as you know the radical first.
reading_mnemonic: Although this kanji has two on'yomi to learn, the pronunciations of those two on'yomi are very similar, so that should make them easier to remember. When you were nine your favorite foods were cookies (く) and cucumbers (きゅう). Yum yum!

meaning_mnemonic: Lucky for you (as is the case with many of the lower-stroke kanji), this kanji is the same as the radical you've already learned. The radical that makes up this kanji is seven and the kanji (which is exactly the same) is also seven. So, if you know the radical, you know the meaning of the kanji as well.
reading_mnemonic: You know this kanji means seven, so let's use that to remember the reading too. Seven is a lucky number, usually, but this time it isn't so good: Seven percent is all she got on her test after she cheated (しち) on it.

meaning_mnemonic: Remember how the radical version of this kanji meant person because it looks like a person with their arms down and their legs spread out? Well this is a person too!
reading_mnemonic: Only one person at Nintendo (にん) complained about the new jeans (じん) policy, and that person was you.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for enter first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means enter as well.
reading_mnemonic: Turns out, after you enter the tent (remember how the person in the radical is entering one?), you're given a new (にゅう) one! Why? No idea, but hey — it's new!

meaning_mnemonic: This isn't exactly the same as the fins radical, but it's close. Sometimes this will happen (where we have to use a slightly "modified radical" version of the original), so it's good to understand that now, early on. In this case, we have fins. How many fins? Eight fins. How do you know that? Because you caught four fish with two fins each.
reading_mnemonic: After you count and smell all eight of your fins, it's time to put them away. You open a large hatch (はち) and put them in. This is where you keep your fins, always putting in eight at a time because that's what the boss wants.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the meaning of this kanji are the same. Both are power.
reading_mnemonic: Who has the most power of anyone? It's the Power Rangers. They are battling their arch enemy Ricky (りき). They defeat him and lock (りょく) him up, so that he can't hurt anyone ever again.

meaning_mnemonic: This cross is the symbol for the number ten. A good way to remember this is to think about all the religions that have crosses and also important sets of tens.
reading_mnemonic: This cross in particular has ten jewels (じゅう) on it. Two on each arm and two in the middle. That's ten jewels!

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is made up of the ground radical (which also happens to be the kanji for "one") and the radical for two. Combine one and two together and what do you get? Three!
reading_mnemonic: Three is the number of chances you get with Santa-san (さん). He has a list, and when you get to three "naughty things" lines, that's it. You're on Santa-san's three strikes and you're out list.

meaning_mnemonic: You find a toe on the ground. It's weird, because it's above the ground, not where toes belong.
reading_mnemonic: Of course when you find a toe above the ground, you want to know where the toe came from. When you examine it, you see a name written on there. This toe belongs to the local clumsy farmhand, Joe (じょう).

meaning_mnemonic: There's the ground, and there's a toe just below it. Yep, you know this means "below" because the ground has a toe below it in this kanji.
reading_mnemonic: You keep digging in the ground for the toe below, but instead you hit something hard and metallic. You try to dig around it, but it's huge. Turns out it's a car (か). Keep digging until you unearth the car below. (Inside, you find the toe you were looking for.)

meaning_mnemonic: The mouth radical and the mouth kanji are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: Do you remember seeing the construction worker こういち earlier in the 工 mnemonic? If you haven't yet, not to worry! For kanji with こう readings (there are a lot of them!) we will use the character こういち every time. He's one of the people who started this website, so we'll do our best in the mnemonics to embarrass him as much as possible. Anyways, remember that whenever you see こう, think こういち. Everyone agrees, the mouth is こういち's best feature. You stare at it lovingly as he whispers sweet kanji readings to you.

meaning_mnemonic: The big radical and the big kanji are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: There's this big guy (that's how you remember the radical, remember?), and he's wearing a huge Tie Dye (たい, だい) shirt. Because he's so huge, the tie dye shirt is also super huge. Everything about him is pretty big, but the tie dye stands out more than anything.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical for woman and the kanji for woman are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: When you think of a woman, think of Jo-Anne (じょ), though she usually goes by just "Jo."

meaning_mnemonic: The mountain radical and the mountain kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic: Think about mountains talking to each other, calling each other by their names and adding the Japanese name-ender san (さん) to each of their names. "Hello, Everest-san." "Oh hi, Fuji-san."

meaning_mnemonic: The river radical and the river kanji are the same as each other!
reading_mnemonic: You're standing next to a river that's actually used as a car wash (かわ).

meaning_mnemonic: The construction radical and the construction kanji are the same! This kanji also means industry, which is what construction is, if you think about it. It's all part of the construction industry.
reading_mnemonic: Every time a kanji uses the こう reading (there are a lot!), we'll use the character こういち. He's one of the people who started this website, so we'll do our best in the mnemonics to embarrass him as much as possible. Like this: You see some construction in front of you. There, standing shirtless (only suspenders and a hard hat) is こういち, looking back at you.

meaning_mnemonic: The dirt radical and the dirt kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: Who spends a lot of time in dirt? Dogs (ど) do! Dogs dig in dirt, they roll in dirt, sometimes they try to eat dirt (which isn't so great).

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical you learned, so it means thousand.
reading_mnemonic: Remember the thousand people going down the slide on a cross in the radical 千? Turns out each one of them was carrying a thousand cents (せん). Go ahead and try to calculate what a thousand times a thousand cents would come out to. It's quite a lot, actually.

meaning_mnemonic: The evening radical and the evening kanji are the same. If you know the radical you know the meaning of the kanji.
reading_mnemonic: The evening is when all the youths (ゆう) come outside to play.

meaning_mnemonic: The child radical and the child kanji are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: The main reading here is し, so to remember it we'll use this mnemonic: There is a child standing in front of you. You look closely at the child but something seems wrong. You rub your eyes and when you open them again, there is a sheep (し) in front of you. A sheep?! You yelp, blink again, and it's back to being a child. Are… are all children really just sheep?

meaning_mnemonic: The small radical and the small kanji are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: This small kanji would be the perfect gift to give to the Shougun (しょう). The Shougun loves little things, and the little kanji represents all of that.

meaning_mnemonic: On the ground you put barbs at the bottom of a slide. This is your special talent. When you go down the slide, you fly right past the barbs like some kind of daredevil. Any normal kid would land on the barbs and get hurt, but you have this talent.
reading_mnemonic: But then people start to say that no human could have so much talent, that you must be a cyborg (さい). Are you really a talented cyborg?

meaning_mnemonic: The radical middle and the kanji middle are both the same. So if you know one, you know the other.
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading for this kanji, we use the word Chewbacca to pull up ちゅう in our memory. If you remember back to the radical 中, a stick was stuck in the middle of the mouth of something. Let's say it was your mouth, and when you look up to see who did it, there stands Chewbacca. He's even doing his Chewbacca yell. And it isn't a stick in your mouth, it's an arrow from his bowcaster. It just so happens Chewbacca's bowcaster looks just like this kanji too. Go figure.

meaning_mnemonic: The five radical and the five kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic: Five is the number of buildings Godzilla (ご) will knock down. Oh, look! There he goes now.

meaning_mnemonic: Just imagine a beast with a lid for a head and fins for feet, running around looking as insane as possible (really imagine it!). When it runs up to you, it shows you the top of its lid-head. On it is written the numbers 666. Why? Because it's a spawn of the devil, and the number six is the devil's number.
reading_mnemonic: Whenever we need to remember the reading ろく we just use the word rock. So, think about the devil and the devil's number. What is often associated with those things? Why, rock (ろく) and roll is. Imagine the lid-head fin-legged beast suddenly blasting out rock music in the middle of his destructive mayhem.

meaning_mnemonic: Here we have a head with a lid in it, near the top. Imagine the top of someone's head being closed by a lid. Open that lid up and peer inside... it's full of yen coins, the currency of Japan. Jackpot! And all those yen coins have a nice round shape, naturally.
reading_mnemonic: What does the word yen sound like? It sounds like えん. Why? because back in the day, Japanese used to have a "ye" sound, but now it doesn't. Instead, it's an "e" sound, which is why yen = えん!

meaning_mnemonic: The radical heaven is the same as the kanji heaven, making this an easy kanji to memorize.
reading_mnemonic: Heaven... nowadays, people aren't all that good. Things have gotten bad. That's why the acceptance rate to get into heaven is only ten (てん) percent!

meaning_mnemonic: The hand radical and the hand kanji are identical in looks and meaning! That should make things easy!
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading て we will use the word "television." You have great hands. Go ahead and look at them. OH MY GOD. You have little televisions (て) on your hands. They are playing the dumbest show you can think of, too, both hands at the same time.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for writing first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means writing as well.
reading_mnemonic: This kanji has more than one important reading you need to learn! But don't worry, here's a mnemonic to help you: You always put writing on your buns (ぶん) to keep them from getting eaten by the bun monster (もん). What kind of writing? Usually it's just an X to show the monster these buns are off-limits. (In fact, it kind of looks like the X part in 文. Hmm…)

meaning_mnemonic: The sun radical and sun kanji are the same, huzzah! Also, if you want to remember day as well, you can just think about how a day is the time it takes for the sun to cross the sky.
reading_mnemonic: There are so many on'yomi for this kanji, but since this kanji is so important and common, you'll end up learning them all eventually whether you want to or not. For now, you're only going to have to learn one of the readings, and that one is にち. The sun is so hot. It focused its rays to take out one man... and that man is Friedrich Nietzsche (にち), famous philosopher. He philosophized one too many things about the sun, so the sun decided it was time he paid.

meaning_mnemonic: The moon kanji is made up of the moon radical. This kanji is also used to mean month.
reading_mnemonic: The moon really gets (げつ) to your guts (がつ). Staring at the moon for too long will give you terrible indigestion, so be careful!

meaning_mnemonic: This is another kanji that is the same as the radical. Both tree and tree are the same in looks and meaning.
reading_mnemonic: You’re walking through the trees, looking at them. They look ominous. Suddenly, you trip and fall. The trees start to mock (もく) you. Even the mocking birds mock you. It’s terrible. It’s painful. You’re being mocked as you pull yourself up off the ground.

meaning_mnemonic: The water radical and the water kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic: Imagine a lake (i.e. a whole bunch of water). When you think of water, you should try to think of this beautiful lake. It’s sunny, the trees smell nice (imagine a tree smell if you can – the more senses you use the better!) and on that tree there is an awesome tire swing (すい). You get onto the tire swing and you are swinging back and forth. The water is right in front of you, and you are able to use the swing to throw yourself into the water. It’s a lot colder than you expected, and you come back to the surface, gasping for breath. The water gets into your mouth and you taste it. How strange, it’s very, very sweet. Imagine the sweetness of the water and how weird it is (really really sweet, this water is).

meaning_mnemonic: The fire radical and the fire kanji are the same as each other.
reading_mnemonic: Whenever we need to remember か, we use the word car. For this kanji, when we think fire, we ought to think of something on fire. What's on fire? It's obviously your very own car (か)! Oh Goddd NOOO!

meaning_mnemonic: The dog radical and dog kanji are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: Every dog likes to eat noodles (いぬ). Like that movie where the dogs share a noodle and end up kissing, right? So when you see 犬, just imagine how those two eat noodles.

meaning_mnemonic: The king radical and the king kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: When you see the king you need to say, "Oh (おう) King! Oh King, oh no, oh why are you looking at me like that? Oh King... you aren't going to chop off my head are you? OH NO!"

meaning_mnemonic: There are two mountains in front of you... and probably a bunch more around you too. You are in a pass, and don't know how to get out. You are frantically looking for the exit before you freeze to death. The most important thing is to find the exit from this mountain range - your life depends on it.
reading_mnemonic: As you're trying to exit this mountain range, you suddenly realize that someone is actually hunting you. What? Make sure to feel that sudden realization. It's crazy. Then, you find the exit and run towards it. Sadly, the hunter is waiting there, and he shoots you (しゅつ) through the leg, knocking you down.

meaning_mnemonic: Narwhal mouths are on the right side of their head. In fact, some people didn't think they had mouths at all because they weren't looking from the right. Rookie mistake. See how the "mouth" radical is to the right of the "narwhal" radical? That should help you remember that this means right.
reading_mnemonic: How did we know to look from the right, though? Because the youths (ゆう) figured it out. Youths think in ways that older people usually don't. That's why they can see the swirls on cereal, hear the music behind noise, and of course, look at things from the right side.

meaning_mnemonic: Imagine contorting yourself in such a way that your mouth now has your legs inside it. You've bent your body in all the wrong ways to achieve this. In fact, if you look at yourself, you look like a square now... You're just a person with four sides.
reading_mnemonic: Now that you have four sides, you look like a four-sided animal: the sheep (し). Look at yourself in the mirror and see an adorable four-sided sheep looking back at you. Imagine yourself with perfectly square wool. (You can only see four sides because mirrors aren't 3D. So you're a flat, cartoonish sheep.)

meaning_mnemonic: Narwhals do construction with their left hands (or flippers, I guess). That's because all narwhals are left-handed!
reading_mnemonic: In their left hands, the narwhals all hold saws (さ). That's because the ice for their homes is already there, so they just need to saw away at them to make the shapes they want. Narwhal construction is actually very simple.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for book first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means book as well. Take note that the second, third, and fourth meanings of this kanji are origin, real, and main. You can figure this out by thinking about how books mainly have their origins in real life.
reading_mnemonic: Books are one of the best ways to hone (ほん) your intellect, you know?

meaning_mnemonic: There is a line on the ground so you stop, making a giant sign pop up that says CORRECT! You obeyed the rules of the road and did the correct thing. Good on you.
reading_mnemonic: You did the correct thing, so here's your reward: a saber (せい) from the Shougun (しょう) himself!

meaning_mnemonic: The rice paddy radical and the rice paddy kanji are the same, making this one super easy to remember, at least meaning-wise.
reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading た, we use the word "taco."

You're in the rice field... but when you lean down to examine the rice more closely, you see that it's not rice that's growing, it's a bunch of little tacos (た), blossoming out of the ground.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical white and the kanji white are the same.
reading_mnemonic: The white team was the first to be able to hack (はく) the white iPhone.

meaning_mnemonic: The eye radical and eye kanji are the same as each other, so now you know them both.
reading_mnemonic: Your eyes are important to you, right? Sadly, one of your eyes is missing right now, because a sheep grabbed it and pulled it out, and is now running away from you, yelling his sheep call.... "Mehhhhhh (め)!"

meaning_mnemonic: The stone radical and stone kanji are the same thing!
reading_mnemonic: You throw a stone through a window... and, now you can see something very sexy (せき).

meaning_mnemonic: The radical stand and the kanji stand are the same thing, so now you know them both.
reading_mnemonic: Think of someone who has to stand up straight for you. These people are pros in hospitality. These are the doormen at the Ritz (りつ).

meaning_mnemonic: You cut the leaf with your sword into ten thousand pieces!
reading_mnemonic: Now that you have ten thousand pieces of tiny leaf paper, you decide to turn them into a manga (まん)! Each little leaf piece will become a panel.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for now first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means now as well.
reading_mnemonic: Right now the condors (こん) are in danger! Not next week, not next year, right now! Haven't you heard that deforestation and pollution are killing all of the condors?!

meaning_mnemonic: The origin radical and the origin kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: The origin of everything can be found in Genji (げん). Genji is the name of the main character in the world's first ever novel, "The Tale of Genji." Picture him as a rich, pretty boy who cares a ton about his looks and gets along really well with all the ladies. He's also really great at poetry, which helps the lady situation.

meaning_mnemonic: You have fins in private. But, you want the world to see them, so you take them public.
reading_mnemonic: You head out into the public where everyone can see your fins, but... things have changed. All people are the same. There are thousands of こういちs walking around, and they all stare at you (though they pretend like they aren't).

meaning_mnemonic: Your head has a person inside it!
reading_mnemonic: You know this kanji means inside, so you can keep thinking about the person that's inside you, running around. You finally discover him, and try to take him out, but before you can, he pulls out a knife (ない) and threatens to cut you if you do anything irrational.

meaning_mnemonic: If you have seven swords, there's only so much you can do with them. The main thing? Probably using them to cut something.
reading_mnemonic: Because having seven swords for yourself is too much, you decide to take the swords and divide them up amongst pairs of people. You cut them into pairs, and give sets (せつ) to everyone who needs them in the village.

meaning_mnemonic: The slide is dry at noon. The sun is brightest at noon, so it dries the morning dew off the slide, making noon the perfect time to slide.
reading_mnemonic: Noon also happens to be the time Godzilla (ご) decided to attack for the same reasons: it's dry and kids are using the slide.

meaning_mnemonic: A narwhal sitting on a stool is your friend.
reading_mnemonic: "Hi friend," says the narwhal. "I must warn you about all the youths." (ゆう)

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical, so this means fat.
reading_mnemonic: Imagine a fat person who loves to sleep on futon (ふと).

meaning_mnemonic: You have a small slide. The thing about small slides is that few people can use them. Not everyone can fit their bum in a small slide — only a few small ones can make it down.
reading_mnemonic: Another reason so few people can use it is that the Shogun (しょう) is trying to go down the slide. We're talking a grown man who's way too big for this little slide, so a few people have to wait behind him — it's a slide traffic jam.

meaning_mnemonic: If you have a bow and a stick you need to pull the two back together to shoot it. If you can't pull it, you won't be shooting anything.
reading_mnemonic: When you pull the bow back, your body strains and you feel an immense heat (ひ) rise inside of you. You keep pulling and the heat grows hotter and hotter.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical heart and the kanji heart are the same. Rejoice and let your heart be free!
reading_mnemonic: The heart, where is it stored in your body? Most people thought it was in the chest, but in reality, your heart is stored in your shin (しん).

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the kanji for direction are the same! Huzzah! There is also another meaning too, though. This can also mean way as well. Think of it this way: When you move in one direction in your life, you are developing your own way. "The way of [your name here]."
reading_mnemonic: What direction do you always know? Which direction do you always want to go? Home (ほう). Something about your home always stays with you, no matter how far away you go. So if you're lost and you don't know which direction to go, just think of home!

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the kanji for cow are exactly the same! That makes it easy to remember, so long as you know your radicals well enough.
reading_mnemonic: Have you ever heard of わぎゅう (wagyu) beef? That ぎゅう is this ぎゅう.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the kanji for father are the same.
reading_mnemonic: Imagine your father is Cheech (ちち) from Cheech and Chong.

meaning_mnemonic: The stop radical is the same as the stop kanji.
reading_mnemonic: You have to stop because there is a sheep (し) in front of you. You try to walk around the sheep, but it moves to stop in front of you again. Every time the sheep stops you stop too.

meaning_mnemonic: Who's someone who's just a mouth with legs? That's your know-it-all older brother, who won't shut up about anything.
reading_mnemonic: You wish you could box your loud-mouth older brother up and send him far away to きょうと. きょうと is super far away from where you currently live, so just ship your older bro off so he can never bother you again.

meaning_mnemonic: You’ve got a winter with lots of ice. But doesn't any winter have lots of ice? Exactly. That's why this is just winter.
reading_mnemonic: Winter is also the time of year you give out presents: "One fu' you, one fu' you and… one fu' you (ふゆ)!"

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical — it means north.
reading_mnemonic: You go north, and notice that everyone has a keytar (きた). You know, those keyboards that people hold and play like a guitar?

meaning_mnemonic: A triceratops is lying out to dry. But it's so big, and it's lying on its side, so only half of it gets dry.
reading_mnemonic: "You're half wet and half dry! I will cut you in half with my laser blaster so you're proper again," a voice says. It is Han Solo (はん), the anti-establishment guy who hates when things aren't even.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for old first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means old as well. Note: This "old" does not refer to people. Think of it as "old things" instead.
reading_mnemonic: Old things are misunderstood by the 子s (こ) of the world. *Note:* Come up with a 子 character you can use for all the こ reading mnemonics going forward. This child will show up many times throughout your mnemonic journey, and it will help if you imagine the same character the whole time.

meaning_mnemonic: You have a private mouth that's a machine. But you have to keep your machine mouth private because it would scare all the non-machine people around you.
reading_mnemonic: To make sure they can't tell what's machine and what's human, you dye (だい) the mouth to make it look like skin. You find dye the same shade as your normal mouth and just slap it on there.

meaning_mnemonic: You're known to get the ailment evening toe, which is when your toe catches on fire after getting really, really hot (imagine this happening, ouch!). The only way to fix it is to cool your toe down, and the best way to do that is to go outside.
reading_mnemonic: You go outside (you’re not supposed to be out there at night!) and you’re accosted by a couple of guys. Then, all of a sudden, Guy (がい) Fawkes jumps from the roof above you and takes them out, then starts running. “Guy Fawkes!” you yell after him!

meaning_mnemonic: You see a manhole lid and a towel, both with the name of a city on them. Decorative manhole lids and souvenir towels — two things cities love to slap their names on, especially in Japan.
reading_mnemonic: This city must have a lot of sheep (し) because, besides the manhole lid and the towel, all you can see are sheep. There are sheep everywhere. It's a sheep city.

meaning_mnemonic: The canopy you use in private is very wide.
reading_mnemonic: You like being wide because it makes you feel like a different person. But not just any person, like a super hero (ひろ)!

meaning_mnemonic: Someone breaks part of your window. Who did this? It was your mother!
reading_mnemonic: Suddenly your mother points her bloodied finger at you and laughs, "Haha (はは)!" She keeps laughing, haha haha haha, over and over. You feel even more alarmed.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for task first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means task as well.
reading_mnemonic: Today, your task is to eat yogurt (よう). It's nutritious, it's delicious, and I'm telling you to do it, so you have to. A task is basically just something you have to do, so that's what this is.

meaning_mnemonic: The world radical and the world kanji are the same, but there is another really important meaning you need to know: generation. Think of it this way: the world is just made up of many different generations of people, plants, and animals all getting along together.
reading_mnemonic: It's your job to protect the world and every generation with your special saber (せい). It was given to you to uphold correctness, and you'll pass it on to the next generation when it's time. Then they'll watch out for the world when you're gone.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical master and the kanji master have the same meanings! This kanji also means main because the master is the main person of a dojo or household or business.
reading_mnemonic: Do you remember back to the radical mnemonic, where the master is floating a water drop above his head? Imagine back to there. Once you do, the most amazing thing happens. The master sends the drop of water into a chute (しゅ) and it goes careening through an intricate series of them.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader of alligators... she's no ordinary leader, that's for sure. She's not a politician, she's not a queen... She's one of the Other Ones, a group of strange, eccentric people who become leaders of animals.
reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading た, we use the word "taco":

Then there's the others of the others. These are the taco (た) worshipers. They're really strange.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader for the ceremony can't come so you need a substitute to replace them ASAP! This kanji has another meaning too. The leader can't come to the ceremony because they forgot what period of time it was. If they think they're in the wrong age, they won't come because they're trying to lead some monkeys in the ceremony instead.
reading_mnemonic: The substitute leader is wearing the wrong color clothes, so you have to dye (だい) them, like they did in the olden ages.

meaning_mnemonic: The forehead of this beggar is on the ground. Except it's not exactly the ground, it's a giant copy machine, and he's making copies of his forehead!
reading_mnemonic: This ground copy machine can only be the work of one person: a shaman (しゃ)!

meaning_mnemonic: If someone tries to dig up dirt on your private life, tell them no thanks, that stuff is in the past. Some things should stay in the past. Not everyone needs to know everything about your life and your past.
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading きょ, we'll use "Little Kyoto." This will differentiate きょ from きょう, which is regular-sized Kyoto. Get it? You decide to bury all this private dirt from your past in Little Kyoto (きょ). That stuff is from when you were just a little 子 (こ) and you don't like to think about it.

meaning_mnemonic: There's a mouth in the ground (in our case, it's a hatch), and inside is some kind of prison you can't quite get to. If you've ever seen Lost, this will sound familiar... on the hatch, there's actually a series of numbers that you don't understand.
reading_mnemonic: "You want to know the number to the hatch?" yells an old voice from inside. You say "yes," and the voice gives you the numbers and you're in! You go down into the prison, where there is one prisoner: Grandpa ごういち. Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち.

meaning_mnemonic: If you want to dry your horns you need to lay them flat. If they aren't flat they'll always be a little damp somewhere and you'll never have a moment's peace.
reading_mnemonic: Being flat isn't enough, so you cover the whole thing in hay (へい). Hay absorbs water, so you add a flat layer of it.

meaning_mnemonic: Take your fingers to the street to hit some people! Street fingers are for curling into a fist. And that street fist wants to do some hitting!
reading_mnemonic: As you hit one chump after another, suddenly your dad (だ) comes marching out of your house. Uh oh. Dad caught you hitting, which, honestly, isn't a very nice thing to do, so he has every right to stop you.

meaning_mnemonic: There's a cross inside your mouth, so the things you say are very pious. Everything you say, you say humbly.
reading_mnemonic: As you're saying all these humble things, you're also mowing (もう) your neighbor's lawn. Your neighbors love you so much, because you're so humble, and you mow their lawn for them.

meaning_mnemonic: What do you get if you lend a spirit your umbrella? Thanks, of course! Especially if that spirit is Totoro, the spirit of the forest.
reading_mnemonic: So what did you receive as a thanks? You open it up, and there's a ray (れい) gun inside!

meaning_mnemonic: The leader is next to the tree. What is he doing? He's leaning against it, resting.
reading_mnemonic: As he rests, he suddenly gets hungry and pulls a cucumber (きゅう) off the tree and bites into it. A good rest isn't complete without some crunchy tree cucumbers.

meaning_mnemonic: If you go down a slide and get dirt on your legs, it must have been the fault of the previous person, aka the person who went down the slide ahead of you. They should've cleaned off their dirty legs before they went down the slide, but they didn't, and now you've got dirt all over your legs too.
reading_mnemonic: Then you realize: the previous person on the slide must've been a centaur (せん). Centaurs track dirt everywhere 'cause they're always galloping around in the wilderness.

meaning_mnemonic: What is the evening mouth? Imagine a mouth that’s up in the night sky. It’s just there, talking, and only comes out at night. It only appears in one area of the world (what area would you choose? Imagine yourself going to that place to see the “night mouth.”), and appears only one month out of the year (more on this in a second). The “evening mouth” is the most famous thing in the _____ area (this is the area you choose). He’s so famous that everybody knows his name (“Evening Mouth.”).
reading_mnemonic: So, when does “Evening Mouth” appear? Turns out, “Evening Mouth” only comes out to talk in May (めい). You know this because it’s just starting to be spring, and when you look around (you’re watching “Evening Mouth” again) you see some spring flowers come up.

meaning_mnemonic: The roof child stands upon the roof, holding up a single letter, a single character, a single symbol for the world to see.
reading_mnemonic: The character that is being shown is "J," which stands for Jesus (じ). The kid wants everyone to see this letter and symbol.

meaning_mnemonic: You have a gun and a cow, which must mean it's that time of the year! Every year on New Year's Eve, you get asked to shoot a cow, as per tradition. You really don't want to though, so you deliberately miss every time.
reading_mnemonic: It seems everyone has caught on to the fact that you deliberately miss every year, so this year you make a nendoroid (ねん) decoy in the shape of a cow.

meaning_mnemonic: When the sun is above the cross, it's time for some people to go church — which is always way too early on a Sunday, am I right? And if you want to get to church early, you need to be fast, otherwise you'll be too late.
reading_mnemonic:
To remember the そう reading we use the word "soul."

When you're forced to get up fast and early you can feel it in your soul (そう). You're so tired and it's so early, your soul cries out, "Please don't make me go this fast this early. I'm gonna leave your body if you keep this up!"

meaning_mnemonic: These days energy is the greatest treasure. Not gold, money, or anything like that. Imagine finding some in a literal treasure chest. As soon as you open it, out bursts the energy in a kind of spirit ball.
reading_mnemonic: As you reach inside the energy spirit ball, you feel something hard inside. It's a large key (き) that gives you access to another treasure.

meaning_mnemonic: There is a leaf growing out of the sun! You fly out into space to check it out and when you get closer you see that it isn't just one leaf, it's a hundred! That makes sense, you wouldn't be able to see just one leaf on the sun from where you were on earth.
reading_mnemonic: You fly closer, counting all one hundred leaves when you hear a strange sound. You take off your space helmet and hear, "GUH HYUCK (ひゃく)!" You know that laugh... it's Goofy! On top of the hundredth leaf is Goofy laughing and waving around. He must have built this leaf tower to get your attention.

meaning_mnemonic: The ear radical and ear kanji are the same in looks as well as meaning.
reading_mnemonic: Put your hand to your ear and sing... "Mimimimimimiiiii!" (みみ) and listen to your tone with your ear.

meaning_mnemonic: Someone's taking tree measurements… Why are they taking measurements of trees? Because they're planning to cut them down to make their village.
reading_mnemonic: They take all the wood back to where they're building their village, and once they construct the village center they paint a mural (むら) on the side of it. The mural is of the forest where they got the trees from, to honor the village's origins.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical for man and the kanji for man are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: When you think of a man, think of dawn (だん), because that man has to get up at dawn to power his rice paddy every day.

meaning_mnemonic: When you see both a rice paddy and a street in the same place, you have the makings of a whole town!
reading_mnemonic: You go to visit this nice little town. But then, there she is... Every time you walk down the street, the street-woman Mrs. Chou (ちょう) arrives to ruin your day.

meaning_mnemonic: All these flowers were planted by your leader with nothing but a spoon. Now the whole place is absolutely full with beautiful flowers. Flowers everywhere.
reading_mnemonic: But for some reason, the leader just can't stop planting flowers... He's going crazy. Maybe it's the pollen? Now there’s only one person that can save him: Hannah (はな).

meaning_mnemonic: The radical see and the kanji see are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: You see something. It's walking towards you, but you need to see better. When the person comes close, you realize "That person is me (み)!"

meaning_mnemonic: The radical for red and the kanji for red are the same thing!
reading_mnemonic: This kanji means red, AKA, also known as, あか.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical for foot and the kanji for foot are exactly the same. That being said, there's also another meaning you should keep in mind, which is sufficient. If you think about it, one foot should be sufficient enough to walk around with if you hop.
reading_mnemonic: What do you wear on your foot? You wear a sock (そく).

meaning_mnemonic: The radical car and the kanji car are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: When we need to remember the reading しゃ, we use "shaman". There's a car. It's the nicest car you've ever seen. Exquisite, beautiful. Wouldn't you be surprised to learn it belongs to a shaman (しゃ)? Well it does. This shaman charges a premium for his shaman services so he can afford fancy cars like this.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical not and the kanji not are the same thing! That makes it easy... Not!
reading_mnemonic:
To remember ふ we'll use the word "fool."

Think of those jokes, where someone says something, then ends with a loud "NOTTTT!" Someone is doing that to you, over and over. What is that person? That person is a fool (ふ).

meaning_mnemonic: The leader samurai didn't become leader by sitting around not taking action. He got to where he is by doing.
reading_mnemonic: He was doing things with sheep (し). He is the leader of the sheep clan, and he was able to do more with sheep than anyone else. That's why he's the leader.

meaning_mnemonic: You put a lid on your father. But, he won't taste good alone, so you mix in some other ingredients. They mingle inside the pot with him.
reading_mnemonic: With a mix of your father and other ingredients mingling in your cooking pot, you lift up the lid... your father pops up. Your father is こういち. He stares back at you with a big smile.

meaning_mnemonic: The meet radical and the meet kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: What better way to meet new people than to start kayaking (かい)! Get into your kayak and just float out into the water. You'll eventually bump into someone else in a kayak and boom, you're meeting someone new!

meaning_mnemonic: You see a triceratops in the distance. But, it's odd. It's perfectly pi shaped (that is, circular, like a pie). Some kind of piceratops, if you will. The reason they are this shape is because they want to absorb as much light as possible. They evolved to be round so they don't have any corners casting a shadow.
reading_mnemonic: As you watch this majestic beast absorbing light, suddenly several dozen feral こういちs burst out from the wilderness, spears in hand. Oh no! Those こういちs are hunting this rare piceratops!

meaning_mnemonic: There's a mustache on the ground. Upon closer inspection, you see that the mustache on the ground is exactly the same as yours!
reading_mnemonic: When we need to remember the reading どう, we use the word "doughnut". While this is already strange enough, you notice something stranger. Over a couple feet away is a doughnut (どう) who also has the same mustache as you (and the one that fell on the ground). The doughnut looks at you for a moment, then scampers off. This doughnut must be a mutant because normally doughnuts don't move.

meaning_mnemonic: There's a mouth inside a mouth. But if you look even closer (not actually, but we're pretending), you can see another mouth inside that mouth... and another one inside of that one! It keeps going and going. Can you count the number of times there's a mouth inside a mouth? This kanji also means revolve too. Think of each "time" a thing happens, it loops back around and comes back to the beginning, revolving around again another time.
reading_mnemonic: If you're having a hard time wrapping your head around the infinite number of times these mouths revolve, just picture yourself in a little kayak (かい) going around and down through the mouths.

meaning_mnemonic: How many evenings are there? There are many.
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading た we use the word "taco." Let's start with the kanji meaning: many. You go outside in the evening (because that's what this kanji is made up of) and are surprised when you're hit by many tacos (た) flying from the sky. For some reason it's raining tacos, and of course you have no idea why.

meaning_mnemonic: What superhero is most like a triceratops? …If you said Wolverine, you're correct! Why is that the right answer? Because the triceratops has three horns, and Wolverine has three blades coming out of his hands. It's obvious, isn't it? But you knew that of course.
reading_mnemonic: Because you got the answer correct, you win a free trip to とうきょう. Congrats!

meaning_mnemonic: You have a gun and you see some windows. What do you think you're going to do with this gun? Of course, you're going to shoot the windows... every single one of them. Each and every one.
reading_mnemonic: Now that every window is broken, you feel pretty stupid because mice (まい) are pouring in through each one. You've made a way for mice to get into your house. That wasn't smart.

meaning_mnemonic: The rice radical and rice kanji are the same in looks and meaning. This kanji can also mean America, maybe because America is covered in rice or fields or something?
reading_mnemonic: A ton of rice is grown in America. And yet you never see rice in American cuisine. So where's all that unused rice going? Actually, it all gets dumped into a big bay (べい). They have too much rice and no place to store it, so they've started using bays to store it.

meaning_mnemonic: In a coffin there's a beggar, doing his begging. But it doesn't work, nobody helps him. So, he just begins to think: Why am I in this situation? How could I have avoided it? How will I get out? Think, dammit, think!!
reading_mnemonic: What does the beggar think of? A thought bubble appears near his head. In it is a picture of こういち! He's thinking that if こういち were here, he'd save him. Oh, if only こういち could save us all!

meaning_mnemonic: The meat radical and meat are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
reading_mnemonic: You know who loves meat? Nick (にく). You probably know a Nick — imagine him eating some succulent meat right now.

meaning_mnemonic: The self radical and self are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
reading_mnemonic: When we need to remember じ we use the word "Jesus." Who said you should always look at your self before tossing stones (or whatever) at others? Jesus (じ) did. So, make sure you look at your own self before being a jerk.

meaning_mnemonic: The color radical and color are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
reading_mnemonic: You already have color on the mind because you know the meaning of this kanji, so think of something colorful about yourself. Imagine your ear (いろ) being a weird color... green, purple, red, whatever. Just make it really bright and standing out.

meaning_mnemonic: The go radical and the go kanji are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: "Oh, did he go again?" When こういち is not around, that's what people often say because he goes to the gyoza (ぎょう) restaurant almost every day. こういち just loves gyoza so much, you always know where he is when he is not home.

meaning_mnemonic: The west radical and the west kanji are the same. Isn't that nice?
reading_mnemonic: You go off to the west. It's the Wild West, even. There aren't many people out here, making it easy to find a niche (にし) for your snake oil business.

meaning_mnemonic: Our leader has a lip ring. Wait, our leader has a lip ring? WHAT??
reading_mnemonic: This leader with the lip ring wants one thing. What is it? A nanny (なに) who can make naan (なん). The leader loves naan because it's soft enough to eat with their lip ring on. And a nanny needs to make it because the leader can't do anything on their own.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader has a book all about the human body. Knowing about bodies is a privilege. One that only leaders get—it helps them control all their subjects, like you.
reading_mnemonic: The leader's body book also taught her about something very body specific: how to tie a tie (たい). You can't have a tie on your body, no no. Those are for the leader and her smart body.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader's key is the key that makes all the other keys. It's sort of like the one ring to rule them all, the one ring to bind them... except with keys.
reading_mnemonic: The leader makes all the keys and puts them in a sack (さく) to distribute them to the underlings, who then cut them into shape with a saw (さ).

meaning_mnemonic: You have a mouth full of two massive drops and… treasure?! Upon closer inspection, they appear to form some sort of diagram!
reading_mnemonic: After decades of analyzing the diagram, scientists found out it leads to… a zoo (ず)?!

meaning_mnemonic: You have a samurai with a flag on a stick. On his flag is the symbol 声, the kanji for voice. Why does he have that there? He feels like his Shogun isn't giving him and his fellow Samurai a voice, so he's brought a flag with the word "voice" written on it to protest.
reading_mnemonic: You decide to join the samurai’s protest for more voice but immediately notice… they’re all 子, eh (こえ)?!

meaning_mnemonic: A samurai has come bearing foreheads and legs that he's trying to sell. He thought it was a waste to leave all his slain enemies on the battlefield, so he gathered up their foreheads and legs to sell on the black market for some extra cash. Hey, no judging! A samurai's gotta sell what a samurai's gotta sell, okay?
reading_mnemonic: If you run into this samurai who sells severed foreheads and legs, you should just say "bye (ばい)!" and get the heck out of there. Actually, if anyone tries to sell you severed body parts — samurai or not — you should probably say bye over and over until you can get away from them.

meaning_mnemonic: There is someone wearing horns, holding a bow, and going down a slide held up by a stick. What type of person do you imagine? I'd say someone who's an immature boy. That would be your younger brother.
reading_mnemonic: Your younger brother loves playing dress-up so much that he's now started dyeing (だい) his hair all kinds of colors.
radical_breakdown: 丷|Horns, 弓|Bow, 丨|Stick, 丿|Slide

meaning_mnemonic: You're walking at night when you discover a lantern covered entirely in hair, making it a very strange shape. In fact, this is a form you'd never expect a lantern to take.
reading_mnemonic: You stare at the shape until you finally recognize it: cake (けい)! Well, it's hairy, glowing cake, but it's still shaped like a big slice of cake.

meaning_mnemonic: The ground is scattered with rice, which will cause the Predator to come because he loves rice. Then once he's gone, the next Predator will come to eat.
reading_mnemonic: When they come, though, they're all disappointed. It turns out it's rye (らい) grains, and rye grains taste terrible. Yuck.

meaning_mnemonic: Plant a spirit in the dirt before you start your company and it will be successful. That's what all the great, old Japanese companies did back in the olden days. That's why companies like Mitsubishi have been around for hundreds of years. They planted a spirit in the dirt to help their company grow, and grow it did!
reading_mnemonic: Where did you learn about this method of company growing? From a shaman (しゃ), of course. Shamans aren't just spouting nonsense, they know what they're talking about. And spirits are right up their shaman alley.

meaning_mnemonic: The say radical and the say kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: If you aren't sure what to say, just think about Genji (げん) and ask yourself, "What would Genji say?"

meaning_mnemonic: The radical run and the kanji run are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: You run and run and run and suddenly you feel your soul (そう) leave your body. Still running, you turn around and see your soul running a few steps behind you.

meaning_mnemonic: Someone on a scooter has an axe, and they're getting near to you really fast! Oh no, they're so close now, you need to get out of here!
reading_mnemonic: As they draw near, you recognize who is riding the scooter: the King (きん) of England! Behind him, a bunch of his guards also on scooters and wielding axes appear and move close to you.

meaning_mnemonic: You have a wild viking child you have to take care of. He won't do anything but study, surprisingly. You can't get him to eat, use the bathroom, or anything else. He just wants to study.
reading_mnemonic: This crazy viking child who prefers study over pillaging (and other viking activities)... the other vikings just stop and gawk (がく) at him when they walk by.

meaning_mnemonic: What was the biggest hole in the construction of the world? The sky. If you think about it, the sky is like a big hole someone forgot to fill in. That's why this kanji also means empty! Makes sense — nothing is more empty than the sky.
reading_mnemonic: The sky is usually empty until clouds stage a coup (くう). Basically you can think of the sky as the site for one coup after another as the weather changes.

meaning_mnemonic: The gold radical and the gold kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: The most gold in the land belongs to the King (きん) of England. In fact, you've never actually met someone with gold, it all goes straight to the King whenever someone finds some. You just have a few pennies to work with.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical for rain and the kanji for rain are the same thing.
reading_mnemonic: What if the rain actually tried to aim (あめ) for you? As in, drops would move out of their normal flight path just to hit you on your head? You'd be a lot wetter, that's for sure.

meaning_mnemonic: The blue radical and the blue kanji are exactly the same. Additionally, this can also mean young. You can remember this because young people have potential as limitless as the blue sky!
reading_mnemonic: You've been feeling really blue. Mostly because your skin, hair, and eyes have all turned blue. It was an out-of-the-blue transformation! But now someone places his hand on your shoulder and points at your saber (せい). It's blue too! You aren't alone!

meaning_mnemonic: You plant your flowers in the light of the sun in the shape of a cross, but it's too hot—the sun is too strong—and you end up with grass. Flowers can't grow in these conditions.
reading_mnemonic: The grass on top is brown and burned from the sun, so you need to take a cool saw (くさ) and hack the tops off. The saw is actually physically cool to the touch, to help heal the grass' sunburned bits. It just happens to look cool too.

meaning_mnemonic: For some reason, you are standing on the sun. It's obviously very hot, but the thing you notice most is the sound of you burning up.
reading_mnemonic: This sound isn't just loud, it's familiar. Finally you place it: onions (おん)!

meaning_mnemonic: A leader with a spoon is a powerful thing. Even something as ordinary as a spoon can create great change in the world when given to the right person.
reading_mnemonic: Then, this hero of yours takes their spoon and says some magic words into it, changing it into a car (か).

meaning_mnemonic: A dirt alligator lives in the earth, not the water. They can swim through the earth itself! Which is pretty scary. You can think of this word as ground too, because that's kind of what earth is made of.
reading_mnemonic: The only way to keep this dirt alligator from dragging you under the earth and eating you is to feed it cheese (ち). That way it won't lead you to a horrific death under the earth by dragging you under and spinning you around until you eat dirt (literally).

meaning_mnemonic: As you dig under the ground you discover a head resting near a mountain, which are both strange things to find beneath the earth.
reading_mnemonic: But, you dig too deep and water flows into where you are. Your only hope is a row (りょう) boat floating off in the distance.

meaning_mnemonic: The hat crowns the king, because all kings must have one.
reading_mnemonic: But, as you're going through all the kings, it turns out not all of them have hats after all. The last one you come to is hatless. He's the king of Zen (ぜん). He has simple clothes and a shaved head, unlike all the other fancy kings standing around nearby.

meaning_mnemonic: A drop hits your mustache. Where did it come from? "Ah, it came from yonder," you say, facing that way.
reading_mnemonic: Who shot this drop at you from yonder? You look over yonder, and see a figure. It is こういち.

meaning_mnemonic: With a roof over her head, a woman can relax. She doesn't have to worry about rain or snow or finding a place to sleep. The roof also happened to be super cheap, so she can even relax about her finances.
reading_mnemonic: As she relaxes, she pulls out the cheapest, most relaxing food in the world: anchovies (あん).

meaning_mnemonic: Think about Japan. Japan is a country made up of islands. They're basically three drop drop drops in the large river that is the Pacific Ocean. These are Japan's states or provinces.
reading_mnemonic: Each state has its own shoe (しゅう) to represent it. The bottom of each shoe is the shape of the state, so when you step it leaves a state-shaped imprint in the ground.

meaning_mnemonic: There are mouths, twenty of them, singing beautiful music together. The music seems to bend toward you through the air.
reading_mnemonic: The twenty mouths make so much music that they literally cloak you (きょく) with it. They cloak you with the music.

meaning_mnemonic: A narwhal and a moon is all you have. Imagine one of each under your arms.
reading_mnemonic: Everything you have (except the narwhal and the moon) were taken from you by a roving gang of youths (ゆう).

meaning_mnemonic: Ice is what you're lacking, so the next thing you need to do is go to the store and see if they have any. Nope, no ice. So, now you go to the next store. Is there ice here? Nope. Next!
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading じ, we used the word "Jesus" - Finally, when you're at the last store in existence, you decide it's time to pray to Jesus (じ), asking for a miracle. He comes down from the heavens with ice in his hands.

meaning_mnemonic: If the yakuza hands you a spoon, death is coming for you. It's the death spoon, a sign that the yakuza is coming to cause your death.
reading_mnemonic: Death comes in the form of a sheep (し). The death sheep works for the yakuza, and kills anyone who has their spoon.

meaning_mnemonic: Just like the radical, the kanji means capital.
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading きょう we use the old capital of Japan, Kyoto, which is spelled きょうと. It was the capital of Japan before Tokyo!

meaning_mnemonic: The mouth of the king extends all the way around him (like in this kanji). Where his mouth reaches, that is his country, give or take a few drops.
reading_mnemonic: Turns out the king of this country loves drinking Coke (こく). Every morning that big mouth of his swallows a whole 2-liter bottle of Coke for breakfast.

meaning_mnemonic: The night radical and the night kanji are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: You call your friend at night and say "Yo, Lou (よる)!"

meaning_mnemonic: Who's that woman pretending to be a jet? That's my younger sister. *Sigh*
reading_mnemonic: Your younger sister is giving some mice (まい) a ride on her back like a jet.

meaning_mnemonic: The only woman in this city is your older sister. She's the only woman surrounded by a bunch of men, but she's following her dreams in the big city.
reading_mnemonic: Your older sister may have moved to the city, but she kept her pet sheep (し) with her. Now the only woman in the city is your older sister, and the only sheep is her pet.

meaning_mnemonic: A long time ago, someone put up a canopy over their fortune telling booth and created the first shop. This store was fortune-based, but since then lots of different stores have popped up!
reading_mnemonic: This shop quickly turned into ten (てん) shops! It was a good idea, after all, so all of the other people selling goods and services decided to copy it and create their own shops. The next day there were ten more.

meaning_mnemonic: The bright radical and the bright kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: What do you say when you see something bright? "Ah (あ)!" Like when you open the curtain and the sunshine hits your eyes, or someone shines a flashlight right into your face. Ahhhh, so bright!

meaning_mnemonic: This is the same as the radical for east, so it means east too.
reading_mnemonic: You see a man walk straight toward the sun rising in the east. It's so bright he can't see anything, so he trips and he gashes (ひがし) his knee on a rock. Yikes… But he gets back up, determined to head east, and, oh no, he gashes his other knee! OK, he should probably give up on going east.

meaning_mnemonic: You stop at a small slide. What were you doing before you stopped here? You were walking.
reading_mnemonic: So, you're walking around, minding your own business, when suddenly something flips up and whacks you in the face. You stepped on the head of a hoe (ほ) and it caused it to swing up from the ground and hit you.

meaning_mnemonic: You go down a street that cuts through a rice paddy and leads to a box. When you open the box at the end of the street, you see it's full of images. Image after image. Drawing, painting, you name it. Someone must have left this box of images here.
reading_mnemonic: Okay, I didn't want to tell you this, but the images are all drawings and paintings of gargoyles (が) and cocks (かく). Male chickens, that is. Turns out that's what you wanted to see most. Don't worry, no one is judging you.

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical — straight as straight can be. It can also mean direct, because when you go straight to a place, you're going there directly. Depending on the context it can even mean fix, since fixing something means straightening out all the messed up crooked bits.
reading_mnemonic: Put food straight into your esophagus without chewing and you will choke (ちょく). You want to get straight to the most important part of eating — the digesting part — but if you don't follow all the intermediate steps, you'll end up choking.

meaning_mnemonic: You take an arrow to the mouth because you know too much. You know some very sensitive information, and someone's sent a bow-slinging enforcer to pin your big blabbermouth shut with arrows.
reading_mnemonic: One of the things you know too much about is the sheep (し) plan for world domination! Yes, you know that sheep are in fact plotting to overthrow humanity and take over the world.

meaning_mnemonic: The long radical and the long kanji are the same! This kanji also means leader, because the longer a person is, the better a leader they'll be. Or maybe it was... the longer they've been somewhere? Whatever, longness = leaderness, you know?
reading_mnemonic: You see a very long person. It's Mrs. Chou (ちょう), who has made herself long, like her street. "I made myself long so I can watch more of the street, my domain. I'm the leader of these streets. Watch yourself not-long person," says Mrs. Chou.

meaning_mnemonic: There are some horns on the ground and a moon knife in front of you. When you try to move, they always rotate around with you, staying right in front. You can't escape these objects, for some reason. This kanji means before too. Something that's in front of you is before you, after all.
reading_mnemonic: You're going crazy with these things in front of you all the time. You finally seek the help of a Zen (ぜん) master, who tells you that meditation will save you from this curse. You try it out, and sure enough, the objects are gone! It worked!
radical_breakdown: 丷|Horns, 一|Ground, 月|Moon, 刂|Knife

meaning_mnemonic: You've seen this as a radical before, and the kanji means the same thing — south!
reading_mnemonic: Think about the south. What's down there? Mean Amy (みなみ) lives down there. Think of the last mean thing she did to you and imagine it while yelling out "MEAN AMYYYYY" at the sky.

meaning_mnemonic: You put a roof over the ground to make your own private patch of dirt. This is your room! That's really all a room is, you know? A covered, private place where you can have some time to yourself.
reading_mnemonic: The only problem with your room is that you can't always be alone. Because of your dad's shih tzu (しつ). The shih tzu likes to come into your room and pee everywhere. Ruining your privacy completely.
radical_breakdown: 宀|Roof, 一|Ground, ム|Private, 土|Dirt

meaning_mnemonic: If you loiter around to poop in winter you never know what could be happening behind you. After you're done you could turn back to see something really crazy that you missed because you took so long to poop in the cold.
reading_mnemonic: You finally look behind you and see Godzilla (ご) and a giant こういち having a violent battle back there!

meaning_mnemonic: In a rice paddy you find a heart and it makes you think. You think a lot of thoughts like, "Whose heart is this? Why is it in a rice paddy? Why am I thinking out loud?"
reading_mnemonic: As you are thinking these thoughts, you spot someone on the edge of the rice field. He really reminds you of someone. But who? That's it! He reminds you of that bartender on The Simpsons. What's his name? You think some more. What is it? Oh! Moe (おも) is his name!

meaning_mnemonic: A tsunami of tongues is coming at you. As it washes over you, you feel each individual tongue moving around on your body, licking you. They make you feel so... lively!
reading_mnemonic: This lively feeling isn't just happening to you, the tongue tsunami is licking it into all of the cats (かつ) in your neighborhood too!

meaning_mnemonic: A tsunami is coming, so you point your gun out the window at it. "You better turn back, sea, or I'll shoot!"
reading_mnemonic: The sea decides it doesn't want to die today, so it turns its tsunami around and goes the other way. You hop in your kayak (かい) and chase after it with your gun, to make sure it actually returns to the sea and doesn't just drown someone else.

meaning_mnemonic: Your fortune boils down to a single point in time. One point in time determines how the rest of your future will go.
reading_mnemonic: As you stare at the point, you watch in awe as it moves to the ten (てん) spot in a long series of numbers.

meaning_mnemonic: You scoop some grains into a ladle to do science. You're doing experiments on these grains in your science course.
reading_mnemonic: Using your science skills, the right temperatures and measurements, you manage to get these grains to grow into a car (か). This is the science department's special car now!

meaning_mnemonic: If you can steal the flowers that adorn a hat worn by an angel, you can use them to make delicious tea. Naturally, angels decorate their hats with only the most aromatic and delicious flowers fit for brewing.
reading_mnemonic: After brewing the tea, you look at the hat again and find a nametag inside that says Chad (ちゃ). You decide that from now on this tea variety will be known as Chad tea, in honor of Chad.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical for eat and the kanji for eat are the same! Lucky you.
reading_mnemonic: Thank goodness, you finally get to eat your meal. You're so hungry. Someone has been starving you and now they've finally given you food. Unfortunately, though, every time you take a bite, you get a shock (しょく) from somewhere.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical neck and the kanji neck are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: The only thing you do with your neck is use it to swallow lots of cool beans (くび). Mm mm. Feel those cool, cool beans sliding down your neck. You don't really taste them, but you know they're there.

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical it comes from. Lack becomes Lack!
reading_mnemonic: To remember けつ, we use the word "ketsup." It's the perfect blend of ketchup and catsup! You're lacking something in your fridge. You look around, trying to find the ketsup (けつ) you lack. You can't find it, because you lack it.

meaning_mnemonic: A giant cross with a mouth stands above you. "I am reason!" it says to you. It is the Cross of Reason.
reading_mnemonic: The reason that this Cross of Reason exists is to combat the youths (ゆう) of the world, who just bring chaos into everything.

meaning_mnemonic: The mouth clan are a group of people. They are the people of a nation.
reading_mnemonic: The mouth clan peoples are a nation of people who use their mouths to say mean (みん) things to other peoples.

meaning_mnemonic: While riding your scooter, you take your sword and cut out an area on the ground. You carefully cut all the sides as you go. This area's all yours now!
reading_mnemonic: As you look down at your area with its sword-carved sides, you suddenly realize there is a hen (へん) pecking at the ground in there. "Um, excuse me, hen, I believe I said this is MY area?!" You try to kick it out, but it hops over your leg.

meaning_mnemonic: When you take your leader's measurements, you realize they're too short, so you attach things to them to make the measurements more impressive. Attach some heels to the shoes, then attach another head on top of theirs. There — perfect measurements thanks to these attachments.
reading_mnemonic: You have to remember the kun'yomi reading of this kanji, and the part you need to remember is つ. So, think of how you would attach something to something else. What would you need? You'd need two (つ) things to put together!

meaning_mnemonic: The lion drops a drop of saliva onto this person from above. The person is in a much worse place compared with where they were before, since they only just recently fell into this pit.
reading_mnemonic: From above there is a loud caw, and a giant eagle (い) swoops down, forcing the lion to back off. The eagle grabs the person with its talons, bringing him into the air! But now he's... in the air being carried by a giant eagle, compared with where he was before, is this really better?!

meaning_mnemonic: That slide is your husband's only fault. He loves that slide, more than you, and it's the only thing you don't like about him.
reading_mnemonic: You try to come up with another fault of his so you can complain, when you see a tiny shih tzu (しつ) trotting by. Oh no! Before you can call out, your husband has fallen off the slide and crushed the poor thing. You hear a sharp yelp and then nothing.

meaning_mnemonic: Your heart has a slide running through it because you want to be certain that the blood is flowing in and out of it smoothly. Given how important this is, you want to be absolutely certain.
reading_mnemonic: To be certain that the heart-slide is working, the doctor who put it there hits (ひつ) you in the chest a few times as a test.

meaning_mnemonic: You're flying in a jet. Even though it's one of the fastest things on earth, your child is sitting in the back asking, "Are we there yet? Are we there yet?" You have to keep responding. "Not yet! Not yet! NOT YET!"
reading_mnemonic: What a selfish kid, right? Well, all he thinks about is "Me (み) me me me me me me me me me me." Hate kids like that.

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji uses a modified jet radical. The front area of the wing is wider than the middle area of the wing. This may seem counterintuitive, but by doing this they can fit so much more jet fuel. The jet zooms off and keeps going for a long, long time, until it reaches the end of the earth.
reading_mnemonic: When you get to the end of the world, you land your jet and put out a few mats (まつ) to sit on so you can view the sights.

meaning_mnemonic: Next to the tree, a lid is put on your father. "Hello child," he says. "This is your new school."
reading_mnemonic: Your new school has other students too. They are all こういちs, though.

meaning_mnemonic: The leaf shaped like an eye only grows in winter. Every other leaf, however, will do the opposite, which is to grow in the summer.
reading_mnemonic: Now it's summertime! What do you do during the summer? You just sit around with your favorite string tying knots (なつ) in it over and over again.

meaning_mnemonic: The house radical makes up the house kanji! Pretty easy. This kanji is also used to mean home, so try to remember that too.
reading_mnemonic: What do you do in your house? You eat eggs (いえ), that's what. You eat eggs three times a day, every day. You really love eating eggs in your home!

meaning_mnemonic: The sun is used in a temple to tell time. They don't have clocks or cell phones, they have sun dials and good old fashioned "looking up and seeing where the sun is right now." This also can mean o' clock, as in "five o'clock" It's used when measuring what time it is in Japanese.
reading_mnemonic: Time in a temple makes you think of Jesus (じ). Specifically, Jesus being able to perform time travel magic. He winks at you, goes back to the dinosaur ages, where he wrestles a T-rex. Then, he goes to WWII era and punches Hitler in the mouth.

meaning_mnemonic: The thread that ties you to your clan is paper. Your papers, that is.
reading_mnemonic: You need this specific paper to prove that you aren't a Commi (かみ), aka a Communist. Or that you are. It really depends on where you want to go and what decade this is.

meaning_mnemonic: What you say to oneself (yourself), you decide to write down. Whether this is in the form of a journal, diary, or blog, you feel the need to record these important thoughts in some way.
reading_mnemonic: You need to protect what you write down and record for yourself with a key (き). These are your special thoughts and feelings, you don't want anyone else to see! Lock them away with a key!

meaning_mnemonic: There's a scooter with your mama carrying a task she needs to get done. You see her pass through, hurrying by to get that task done.
reading_mnemonic: As you watch your mama pass through the house, she yells, "YOU HAVE TO DO THIS TASK TOO (つう)!" Too?! Oh no, now you have to do it too. Hurry up!

meaning_mnemonic: There's a lid on your mouth and mustache, covering up all your talking holes. This is because you kept saying how tall and expensive you are.
reading_mnemonic:
"I am taller and more expensive than you." 

You're saying this because there are some こういちs in the room, and you want to make them feel inferior (you're a こういち hater). You keep comparing your height to the こういちs in the room, and you keep checking price tags. Then you tell them you're taller and more expensive than they are.

meaning_mnemonic: You keep your bow private because it's made of insects, meaning it's extremely strong. Insect bodies are really durable, so they make for super strong bows. That's why you have to keep this one private — it's simply too strong to let others get ahold of.
reading_mnemonic: You had this strong bow made especially for you in きょうと. きょうと is famous for their strong bows, so if you ever want another, you know where to go.

meaning_mnemonic: A teacher in winter is happiest because they get to teach! The kids can't go out and play because it's too cold. They all have to come in and stay warm as the teacher teaches!
reading_mnemonic: Teachers can teach the most about Japan in winter by going to きょうと. きょうと is where all the old temples and history of Japan is centered. And it's really gorgeous when it snows.

meaning_mnemonic: The king's village is the reason he's king. Without the village there would be no reason to have a king in the first place.
reading_mnemonic: You can't have reason without re (り).

meaning_mnemonic: Sew thread through your top hat and to the top hats of other people you know and you'll turn into a group of top hat wearing people. You're all connected by the thread now, so everyone will assume you're a group, even if that's all you guys have going for yourselves.
reading_mnemonic: Everyone in this group loves cumin (くみ). You know, the spice or seed. The group take off their top hats and fill them with cumin. You're officially a group for lovers of cumin.

meaning_mnemonic: Your boat has fins and a mouth! It's still a boat though.
reading_mnemonic: This boat belongs to the centaurs (せん). That's probably why you've never seen a boat like it before.

meaning_mnemonic: Use a scooter to travel the circumference of the world and it will take you a full week. Seven whole days!
reading_mnemonic: If you want to scoot for a week, you'll need shoes (しゅう). Good shoes too, not sandals or high heels or boots. Solid, high quality shoes, so you don't fall off the scooter and hurt yourself.

meaning_mnemonic: When rain falls on Wolverine, it turns to snow. He's so emotionally distant and cold that the rain freezes into snow as soon as it gets near him.
reading_mnemonic: You're concerned for Wolverine's mental health. Him being so emotionally cold that he turns rain to snow means you keep (ゆき) asking if he's okay. But that only makes him want to be more distant.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical fish and the kanji fish are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: You catch a fish. As you pull it out of the water, it starts yelling and pointing: "GO!" (ぎょ). "GO GYO GYO GYO!" There's a huge cruise ship coming right towards your little fishing boat. No wonder the fish was yelling GO at you.

meaning_mnemonic: The bird radical and the bird kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: Think of a run-of-the-mill bird, whatever comes to mind for you first is fine. Then, your lovely bird swells. The shape of a face, then a hand, start stretching the bird apart until it explodes outward. Covered in blood and feathers is Mrs. Chou (ちょう).

meaning_mnemonic: The radical black and the kanji black are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: You're in a completely black room. There's no way out, and you can't see. The room starts to fill with liquid. It gets in your mouth. You taste it. It's Coke (こく)! Mm, tasty Coke.

meaning_mnemonic: The branch radical and the branch kanji are the same! This kanji also means support. To remember it, think about a tree with lots of branches. The branches support each other and the trunk of the tree. If you were to climb the tree, the branches would be able to support your weight too!
reading_mnemonic: You're happily sitting on this branch, letting it support all this weight, when a sheep (し) starts to climb the tree. A very, very big sheep. Uh oh... no no, sheep. If you get on this branch it won't be able to support all this weight!!!

meaning_mnemonic: The leader of the masters gets to choose the place they dwell. So they reside in a huge mansion on the top of the mountain, surrounded by all the other masters in their smaller dwellings.
reading_mnemonic: She needs this big place to dwell so she has somewhere to store all of her jewels (じゅう). Masters always have lots of fancy, expensive things, and she has jewels.

meaning_mnemonic: With top hat power, you're able to help anyone.
reading_mnemonic: The person you help with your top hat power? It's Jo-Anne (じょ).

meaning_mnemonic: You're in a cage and you've been shot by an arrow. Obviously things are looking pretty bad. You need some medicine if you hope to live.
reading_mnemonic:
When we need to remember the sound い we use the word "Eagle."

You need your medicine really bad. Then, you look up. There's an eagle (い) flying overhead. He has a package. It's medicine! You're saved!

meaning_mnemonic: Wolverine is going down a slide and from your mouth you scream, "Hey, buddy! Watch it with that slide, it's really fast and you might hurt yourself, buddy!" You're a really good buddy to Wolverine. He also happens to be the local ruler of these lands. You make it a habit to befriend the local strongmen, just in case… No wonder you're so buddy-buddy with all the rulers around here.
reading_mnemonic: As you're about to embrace your buddy Wolverine, a coonhound (くん) tackles him off the slide, and bites him in the process.

meaning_mnemonic: Writing and measurement stand versus one another. Writing is all about feeling and expression. Measurement is about cold hard numbers. Yep, in this world writing people are basically the opposite of measurement people. Which side are you on?
reading_mnemonic: Whenever it's you versus someone else, you wear a tie (たい). Naturally, your tie is always the opposite color of your opponent's tie. Kinda like how political rivals wear different color ties when they debate. It's pretty silly, but at least your tie makes it clear that it's you versus them.

meaning_mnemonic: Your nation's flag sits on top of a caped mouth. This is the symbol for the "Bureau of Secret Things." It's a special department of your government made to keep things hidden.
reading_mnemonic: The bureau's best-kept secret is cloaking devices that cloak you (きょく) with the press of a button.

meaning_mnemonic: You loiter around with a weapon because you're currently doing your service and duty to your country. You're standing guard outside, waiting just in case something will happen.
reading_mnemonic: You're about halfway through your service, when a yak (やく) walks by. It stops directly in front of you and grunts. "Excuse me, Mr. Yak, but it's my duty to escort you away from my country."
